source.version: Published conference paper (version of record) in the proceedings of the 2025 7th International Conference on Computer Science and Technologies in Education (CSTE), IEEE, printed pages 661-665, DOI 10.1109/CSTE64638.2025.11091881; IEEE Xplore download dated October 05, 2026.
source.title_on_document: Empower or Disempower: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on College Students' Creativity

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material, online appendix, data, or code.

paper_design_summary: 113 undergraduates at a university in Gansu Province, China, were randomly assigned to draw an alien for 10 minutes either with the Kimi.AI chatbot open on a computer (58) or without any AI tool (55). Two independent coders rated each drawing for overall creativity (7-point scale), similarity to Earth creatures, and atypical features, following Maddux and Galinsky (2009). A brick alternative-uses test given before assignment served as a baseline check.

studies.label: Lab experiment: draw an alien with or without Kimi.AI

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of the generative AI tool Kimi.AI (web interface pre-opened) versus no AI tool while drawing an alien
assignment.quote: Next, the participants were randomly assigned to either the group using GAI tools or the group not using such tools.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 663), Section II.B Experimental Procedure

arms.name: GAI group (experimental group)
arms.description: Drew an alien for 10 minutes in a computer-equipped laboratory with the Kimi.AI web interface pre-opened, after a brief introduction on how to operate it.

arms.name: No-GAI group (control group)
arms.description: Completed the same 10-minute alien-drawing task independently without GAI tools.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper says 113 students were recruited and randomly assigned; Table I (group composition, N=58/55, demographics collected right after assignment) and Table II (outcomes, Yes N=58, No N=55) give the same arm sizes. The paper never gives a separate count at assignment, so the randomized counts rest on Table I.
participants.who: Undergraduate students at a comprehensive university in Gansu Province; mean age 19.71 (SD 0.89); 55 male, 58 female
participants.quote: A total of 113 college students were recruited for the experiment, with an average age of 19.71 years (standard deviation = 0.89), including 55 males and 58 females.
participants.locator: PDF p. 2 (printed p. 662), Section II.A Study Design; PDF p. 3 (printed p. 663), Table I (N=58/55); PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Table II

ai_tool.name_model: Kimi.AI (Kimi AI chatbot; model version not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: The GAI group worked in a computer lab with the Kimi.AI web interface pre-opened and received a brief introduction and instructions on how to use it; the paper does not describe how participants used it during the drawing task or record their prompts.

task.description: Structured imagination task adapted from Maddux and Galinsky (2009): imagine visiting a planet in another galaxy inhabited by aliens and draw a picture of the aliens living there.

outcomes.name: Overall creativity of the alien drawing (Total Creativity)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two independent coders, unrelated to the experiment (expertise not stated), rated each drawing on a 7-point scale (1 = not creative at all, 7 = highly creative); scores of the two coders averaged; ICC = 0.87.

contrasts.reported: Total Creativity: Yes N=(58) M 6.03, SD 0.90; No N=(55) M 4.71, SD 1.34 (Table II). Text: t (113) = 6.20, p = 0.002, d = 1.16.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B Creativity and Table II

outcomes.name: Similarity to Earth creatures (Similarity to Terrestrial Life)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two coders; two items (similarity to humans, similarity to other Earth animals), each on a 7-point scale; scores of the two coders averaged; ICC = 0.63. Higher similarity means a less novel drawing (inverse novelty, as in Maddux and Galinsky 2009). The printed means (12.87, 10.90) exceed 7, so the two items appear to be summed; the paper does not say.

contrasts.reported: Similarity to Terrestrial Life: Yes N=(58) M 12.87, SD 0.75; No N=(55) M 10.90, SD 1.23 (Table II). Text: t (113) = 10.33, p <0.001, d = 1.93. Direction refers to the printed similarity score: GAI drawings were MORE similar to Earth creatures, i.e. less novel on this measure; the creativity-signed effect is negative.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B Creativity and Table II

outcomes.name: Atypical features of the alien drawing (Atypical Characteristics)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two coders; five items on sensory organs and body characteristics (absence of organs or body parts, unusual quantities, uncommon shapes, unusual functions, special abilities); scores of the two coders averaged; ICC = 0.91.

contrasts.reported: Atypical Characteristics: Yes N=(58) M 3.68, SD 1.03; No N=(55) M 2.08, SD 0.77 (Table II). Text: t (113) = 9.27, p = 0.005 and d = 1.76.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B Creativity and Table II

company_involvement.description: Kimi.AI is the tool tested; the paper states no company involvement. Funding: Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (31920250129).

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to Kimi.AI versus no AI (PDF p. 3, Section II.B); 113 students analyzed, 58 versus 55 (Tables I and II); outcomes are coder ratings of the drawings produced with AI available. Caveat: the paper says the two groups 'were tested separately' and in different rooms (computer lab versus not), so condition is confounded with session and setting.

one_line_finding: Students who drew an alien with Kimi.AI available received higher overall creativity ratings than students without AI (6.03 vs 4.71 on a 7-point scale; t(113) = 6.20, p = 0.002, d = 1.16) and higher atypicality scores, but also higher similarity to Earth creatures (PDF p. 4, Section III.B and Table II).
open_questions: The text in Section III.B mislabels arms: it says 'The unused group novelty score was higher (M = 6.03 ...) than in the unused group (M = 4.71 ...)' and similarly for similarity; Table II assigns 6.03 and 12.87 to the GAI (Yes) group. I followed Table II.

Similarity to Earth creatures is higher in the GAI group (12.87 vs 10.90), which by the Maddux and Galinsky logic means less novel drawings, yet the paper counts it as evidence that GAI enhances creativity. Its scale (two 7-point items, means above 7) is not explained.

Reported statistics are internally inconsistent: t(113) degrees of freedom for two groups of 58 and 55 should be 111; p-values do not match the t values (t = 6.20 with p = 0.002; t = 9.27 with p = 0.005; baseline AUT t = 4.09 with p = 0.06 called not significant); enjoyment is printed as 't (113) = 1.21.22'. The extraction phase should recompute from Table II means and SDs rather than trust the printed t, p, or d.
The AUT scoring text says the originality score was 'the average of the three raters' scores' while naming two psychology experts.

The paper says the groups 'were tested separately' (PDF p. 2, Section II.A); whether randomization was at the individual level with group sessions, and how the drawing was done (paper or computer), is not stated.
Table I prior-experience rows sum to 58 and 65, not 58 and 55, and include an unlabeled row; arm sizes rely on the table headers and Table II.
notes: Pages: PDF pages 1-5 equal printed pages 661-665. A pre-assignment baseline AUT (brick uses; fluency, originality, flexibility scored by two psychology experts) was used only as a balance check (PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 662-663); it is not an outcome. Self-reported familiarity, enjoyment, and motivation (7-point Likert) were collected after the task and are not outcomes (Table II). No diversity outcome is reported. The search record's guess of unclear assignment is resolved: the paper states random assignment.
